sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.

AW-0 is an agentic world action model that unifies code-based planning with world action modeling by jointly denoising skill programs, future video, and control trajectories. An agentic pipeline discovers reusable skills and annotates robot and human demonstrations with programs for both pretraining and downstream fine-tuning. The resulting policy achieves strong performance on both parallel-gripper and dexterous-hand tasks.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Learning-based robotic manipulation has progressed from small task-specific visuomotor policies over decade ago to broadly supervised foundation models that connect perception, language, and action (Levine et al., 2016; Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Bjorck et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Black et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). In parallel, self-supervised video prediction has long been valued as learning signal to model the world: image inpainting extended to video prediction led to action-conditioned video predictors that can imagine the future before committing to an action (Pathak et al., 2016; He et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2022; Finn et al., 2016; Assran et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026). World Action Models (WAMs) couple visual prediction with visuomotor policies, grounding control in representations of how the physical world evolves (Ye et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). This predictive grounding is particularly valuable for complex manipulation, where successful execution depends on anticipating object motion, contact, and the consequences of low-level actions. Yet predicted video and action chunks do not by themselves specify how long-horizon task should be decomposed: which reusable skills to invoke, how to parameterize them, or how to compose them across subtasks. Predicting the world and/or actions in general can also be expensive, especially as it can be difficult to establish limits on how many degrees of freedom need to be world modeled (or teleoperated, in the supervised setting). Agentic robot systems provide complementary structure to WAMs: programmatic harness that selects reusable skills and tools, binds them to the current scene, tracks progress, and replans as observations change (Liang et al., 2023; Fu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). This programmatic representation makes the structure of multi-step tasks explicit, specifying which skills and tools to invoke, with what arguments, and in what sequence. Yet agentic robotics often lacks predictive grounding in real-world physical dynamics and does not leverage learned model of how the world will change as the robot acts. We advocate for an architecture that combines the foresight and action execution of WAMs with the cognitive efficiency, reusable skills, and potential for future self-improvement of agentic robotics. We propose AW-0, an agentic WAM framework that incorporates code-based planning and generation directly into world action modeling via grounded code expert that harnesses broad programming priors to synthesize modular skills featuring explicit parameters and control logic. Code guides synchronized video and control modules within mixture-of-transformers architecture, simultaneously denoising discrete code structures, predicted visual observations, and low-level motor commands. We first show that such agents can be realized by adding code expert to WAM, leveraging multisensor action and code generation in planning stage. We develop modular generation framework: planning via code generation significantly improves WAM performance, by appropriately conditioning the long-horizon generations required for complex robotic tasks. An automated curation pipeline extracts systematic routines into reusable program libraries, mapping code segments directly onto robotic and human video trajectories. This approach bridges high-level semantic reasoning with predictive physical dynamics, establishing unified language for compositionality across distinct environments and tasks. We further demonstrate agentic skill reuse via hybrid deployment strategy that selects between raw action chunk execution and programmatic skill invocation. Empirical evaluations across RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks and physical bimanual setups show substantial performance gains compared to standard VLA and WAM baselines, highlighting programmatic code as an effective structural backbone for predictive planning, skill discovery, and embodied robotic control. Our primary contribution is the conceptualization and realization of agentic robotic skills within world action model framework, showing that code generation improves action prediction in the world model, and that the code generated from the world model can be re-used in an agentic framework. Specific novel contribution elements include: mixture-of-transformers framework integrating code expert into world action models via simultaneous denoising of code, video, and control; an automated agentic pipeline designed for program annotation and skill discovery; dataset of such structured skill programs; and hybrid execution policy that dynamically toggles between programmatic skill invocation and direct deployment of action chunks from the WAM action expert. 2 Figure 2: AW-0 Framework. AW-0 includes Mixture-of-Transformers backbone with three experts generating code, video and action, respectively, which are denoised jointly, with video and action under continuous flow matching and the code under discrete masked diffusion.

Each 3 expert keeps its own attention projections (WQ, WK, WV , WO), layer normalizations, and FFNs, communicating through masked joint attention at every transformer layer. The attention mask is bidirectional within each expert and blockwise causal across experts, following the order of code, video and action. Current multi-view observations are encoded into visual tokens and prepended to the instruction and program tokens to ground skill planning in the scene. Video and Action Experts. The video expert uses video DiT initialized from CosmosPredict2.5 (NVIDIA, 2025b) to model VAE-encoded future frames conditioned on observed frames, while separate action DiT generates continuous action chunks. We use α = 0.5 and leave code-mask sampling unchanged. 2.3 AGENTIC CODING IN WAM Automatic Annotation Pipeline. We propose an automatic annotation pipeline (Figure 3) that annotates the training data with skill planning code in three stages. We first sample one episode per task and use Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026) to write subtask-level skill programs against predefined declaration-only APIs, while Claude Code running Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026) acts as coordinator that distills recurring, task-general skills. We then freeze the skill library and re-annotate the sampled episodes with the finalized vocabulary, forming cache of reusable subtask-to-program mappings. To annotate the remaining corpus, we reuse cached program when the subtasks contact and motion pattern matches an existing entry; otherwise, the coding agent generates new annotation and adds it to the cache. See Appendix for further pipeline details. 4 Figure 3: Automatic Annotation Pipeline. Coding agents generate subtask-level programs using predefined primitive APIs and available skills, while coordinator distills recurring patterns into library of reusable skills across tasks. With the library frozen, we annotate the corpus by reusing cached code when contact and motion evidence match and generating new labels otherwise. Code Usage in Model. Annotated programs define the interface through which the code expert plans. During training, the code stream concatenates conditioning prompt and the active slice, short block of primitive or skill calls. Only the slice is corrupted by the absorbing-mask process of Eq. 4 and supervised by the masked-token loss. At each replanning point, the policy rebuilds the prompt and appends canvas of mask tokens. The canvas is decoded jointly with the video and action states over the denoising steps, committing the G/T most confident masked positions per step. By default, the decoded slice is not executed. It serves as subtask plan that conditions the action expert through joint denoising, while the predicted action chunk drives the robot. Memory Cache. Since single observation is often insufficient to reveal task progress, the code expert receives compact cache of the slices generated so far. The history slices are compressed into learnable memory slots and read back as prefix tokens before the prompt in the code stream. During training, the buffer holds the preceding annotated slices, replaced with probability by the models own predictions. At inference, it is reset per episode and grows with each decoded slice. Hybrid Actions. We additionally explore an inference mode in which the decoded code slice is executed in the manner of Code-as-Policies (CaP) against library of perception and control primitives, and the executed actions are integrated with the direct actions of the action expert. At deployment, the two channels are arbitrated at every replanning point: the decoded slice takes over the current stage only if it passes set of validity and progress checks; otherwise the action chunk from the same forward pass drives the robot until the next replan. See Appendix for the full algorithm. 2.4 TRAINING RECIPE We first pretrain AW-0 on approximately 2,000 hours of YAM robot data and approximately 1,000 hours of egocentric human manipulation data to learn general unified generative prior. sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025) and 8 real-world tasks spanning parallelgripper and dexterous-hand embodiments, assessing language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, as well as the robustness benefits of hybrid execution in variant scenarios. Baselines. We compare four baselines: (1) π0.5 (Black et al., 2025), state-of-the-art VLA with strong semantic reasoning; (2) EgoScale (Zheng et al., 2026), VLA pretrained on large-scale egocentric human data; (3) DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026), WAM jointly generating future video and actions; and (4) WLA (Yang et al., 2026), an autoregressive model jointly predicting textual subtasks, subgoal images, and actions. All baselines and the default AW-0 configuration use the same task-specific demonstrations for post-training and follow the same evaluation protocol. The simulation hybrid configuration uses separately collected CaP-generated demonstrations, as described below. Baseline implementation details are provided in Appendix C. 3.1 SIMULATION EXPERIMENT Benchmarks. We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0. Following the training-data requirements specified on the official RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard1, we train on 50 clean demonstrations per task (2,500 episodes in total) and evaluate under the benchmarks two settings: clean, with clean tabletop, plain background, fixed lighting, and no distractors; and random, with domain randomization over background and tabletop textures, lighting, tabletop height, and distractor objects. We report the mean success rate over 50 rollouts per task. Hybrid Evaluation. We additionally evaluate AW-0 in the hybrid mode, in which the training demonstrations are collected by executing CaP programs written against set of CaP-X-style (Fu et al., 2026) primitive APIs that we develop for RoboTwin 2.0. The programs are written automatically by Claude Opus 4.8, following the agentic framework of ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026). Main Results. Table 1 and Figure 4 report the results on RoboTwin 2.0. The two inference modes exhibit complementary strengths. Overall, AW-0 achieves the highest average success rate of 50.7% across both settings, outperforming all baselines including models designed for broad generalization. The advantage comes mostly from the clean setting, where AW-0 reaches 80.8%, exceeding the strongest baseline WLA (64.8%) by 16.0 points. We conduct real-world experiments on two platforms: the YAM station, fixed-base bimanual setup with two 6-DoF arms and parallel grippers, and the TianjiSharpa platform, bimanual robot with two 22-DoF Sharpa dexterous hands. Both platforms observe three RGB views and act in the unified 64-D stateaction space defined in Appendix A. Further details on the robot setups are provided in Appendix D. Evaluation Protocol and Metrics. We use 100 demonstrations per task for post-training and evaluate on the 8 real-world tasks in Table 2, 4 on each platform, with 3 16 rollouts per task (3 training seeds, 16 evaluation rollouts per seed) under randomized initial object poses. Task definitions, evaluation settings, and per-task scoring rubrics are provided in Appendix E. Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis. As shown in Table 2, AW-0 achieves the highest average rubric score across both embodiments, outperforming the strongest baseline by 25.1 points. Two observations emerge. Language following and semantic reasoning: AW-0 outperforms the baselines strongly on Arrange Fruits and Flip Scoreboard, which require instruction-specific object selection and counting, respectively. The VLA baselines, particularly π0.5, also show relatively strong semantic understanding, while the WAM baselines are less reliable on these properties. These results suggest that code-based planning strengthens the language-following and semantic reasoning of world action models. Robust skill execution: On contact-rich and dexterous tasks, DreamZero outperforms π0.5 on Replace Lightbulb and Deal Poker, where predicting future states provides stable physical-dynamics features for action prediction. AW-0 further outperforms these baselines by combining guidance from generated skill programs with predictive representations of physical dynamics, aligning skill-level planning with continuous control. See Appendix for further analysis. Hybrid Execution in the Real World. We further evaluate hybrid execution on Fold and Stack Towels with the YAM platform based on Algorithm I, comparing it against action-chunk execution under the same post-trained model and evaluation conditions. Under the same task rubric, hybrid execution achieves 90.6%, compared with 84.4% for action-chunk execution, while the direct execution steps of code further enhance the models reasoning capabilities in distinguishing stacking order and action stability. Full programs outperform comment-free code on all 8 shared tasks, suggesting that explanatory language helps connect program structure with task intent. sections.title: 4 RELATED WORK
sections.content: World Action Models (WAMs). World models predict future observations and have recently emerged as powerful paradigm for robot manipulation, serving as learned simulators and data generators for policy learning (NVIDIA, 2025a;b; Gao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024; Jang et al., 2025). Building on this progress, World Action Models (WAMs) unify future prediction and action generation, through joint video-action diffusion (Ye et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025), expert-based architectures (Bi et al., 2025; Cai et al., 2026), or direct adaptation of pretrained video models into policies (Kim et al., 2026). Recent WAMs further couple autoregressive sub-task prediction with future-state modeling and action synthesis (Yang et al., 2026) or dynamically update subtask instructions to condition video and action generation (Tang et al., 2026). However, existing WAMs lack structured semantic guidance and explicit skill invocation, limiting their ability to perform complex semantic planning and structure predicted dynamics into actionable behavioral abstractions. Agentic Robotics. Early work composed perception and control APIs into executable closed-loop behaviors without policy training (Ahn et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023). Later systems generate full Python programs over perception APIs (Huang et al., 2023; Mu et al., 2024; Goldberg et al., 2025), and executable code has proven stronger action space for LLM agents than text (Wang et al., 2024). With the rise of coding agents, program synthesis has become explicitly agentic, with recent systems iteratively writing, executing, and repairing control programs (Lu et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026). Frontier models now also act as controllers themselves, reasoning over instructions and feedback and driving robots directly through native tool calls and learned primitives (Shi et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Gemini Robotics Team, 2025a;b). In all of these systems, the 9 agent controls the robot from outside the policy and is bounded by the primitives it can call. We instead bring code inside an end-to-end model as high-level planning interface and further explore how the generated code can be executed to complement the models own actions at test time.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present AW-0, an agentic world action model that integrates code-based skill planning with predictive dynamics and continuous control. Through joint denoising, the code expert provides structured semantic guidance for video and action generation. An automated annotation pipeline enables learning this planning interface from large-scale robot and human demonstrations. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation with YAM and dexterous hands demonstrate improvements in language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, with hybrid execution further enhancing robustness. These results establish unified foundation for future work on skill reuse and iterative interaction between programmatic planning, world prediction, and execution, providing potential agentic system foundation that continually interacts with and learns from environments.

sections.title: A MODEL AND TRAINING DETAILS
sections.content: We implement the AW-0 architecture using three modality-specific experts coupled by masked joint attention. All experts have 28 transformer layers and project their queries, keys, and values into common 2,048-dimensional attention space. The code expert receives current visual observations and language instructions, the video expert attends to the code stream, and the action expert attends to both. Tables 5 and 6 summarize the architecture and the pretraining configuration. State and Action Representation. Both YAM robot data and egocentric human data are mapped into shared 64-dimensional stateaction space. Each side contains 9-dimensional end-effector pose (3D of x, y, position and 6D rotation representation), 22 dexterous-hand joint angles, and one parallel gripper width, giving 2 (9 + 22 + 1) = 64 dimensions. States are all absolute; while action chunks use end-effector pose deltas relative to the first frame of the chunk, with absolute gripper targets for YAM and absolute hand-joint targets for human demonstrations/dexterous hand. Dimensions unused by an embodimentthe hand-joint blocks for YAM and the gripper dimensions for human demonstrationsare set to zero and left unnormalized. All remaining dimensions are normalized using per-dimension 1st and 99th percentiles. Initialization and Trainable Components. We initialize the video DiT from Cosmos-Predict2.52B (NVIDIA, 2025b) and the action DiT from scratch before joint pretraining. The code expert initializes its token embeddings, layer normalizations, FFNs, and vocabulary head from SDAR1.7B (Cheng et al., 2025) and freezes them, while training its MoT attention projections and modulation parameters. The Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025) vision tower is frozen, with trainable merger mapping visual features to code embeddings. We replace the original VAE with frozen Wan2.2 (Wan et al., 2025) VAE with 48 latent channels and reinitialize the video DiTs input and output projections. The video DiT uses 1 2 2 latent patches and multi-view 3D RoPE. Video and action experts use precomputed Cosmos-Reason1 language embeddings. Downstream adaptation transfers shape-compatible parameters from joint pretraining and reinitializes action and state projections when embodiment dimensions change. Table 5: Expert Architectures and Shared Visual Inputs. Images are sampled at timestep offsets 0, 4, . . . , 32, giving nine frames per view; only the first frame is used as observation conditioning. The code experts visual encoder also receives only this first frame from each view. At 224 320 resolution, spatial merging produces 70 visual tokens per view. The code expert uses the Qwen3-family tokenizer of the SDAR checkpoint. Its 512-token training budget applies to the instruction and program together, with the 210-token visual prefix added separately. At inference, the default program canvas contains 128 tokens. Visual-prefix, instruction, and padding positions are excluded from the standard masked-program loss. Table 6: Generation and Pretraining Settings. Downstream overrides are given in the text. Video noise resampling follows Section 2.2. The pretrained variable is upre = 0.999b, where Beta(7, 1); training samples are drawn from = 0.5ppre + 0.5U (0, 1). The video objective uses the pretrained-density weight, while action and code losses use the uniform-reference weight. Action noise levels and code-mask ratios are sampled independently of the video variable. At least one program token is masked in every nonempty training target. The pretraining recipe additionally replaces the instruction and program inputs with mask tokens for 15% of training batches, retaining the visual prefix. The default decoder progressively commits high-confidence code predictions across the full joint trajectory. Early completion is controlled by ρ < 1, separate decoding-time choice that does not change the training mask distribution. Latency is measured end to end on an NVIDIA RTX 5090, including visual encoding, joint denoising, video decoding, and action postprocessing. Downstream Optimization. Downstream runs use the same optimizer, warmup schedule, and mixed-precision settings as pretraining, with task-specific batch sizes and training budgets. For both YAM and TianjiSharpa, we fine-tune AW-0 for 20 epochs using 100 demonstrations per task. The YAM configurations use per-GPU batch size of four, one gradient accumulation step, learning rate of 104, and weight decay of 102. The RoboTwin configuration uses two 8-GPU nodes with per-GPU batch size of 6 and one accumulation step, giving an effective batch size of 96, learning rate of 2 104, weight decay of 102, and budget of 100,000 optimizer steps. These settings are distinct from the larger pretraining batch in Table 6.

sections.title: B ANALYSIS ON PRETRAINING DATASET
sections.content: B.1 PRETRAINING DATASET STATISTICS We pretrain AW-0 on the union of two real-world manipulation datasets: YAM and Egocentric Human data. The YAM corpus contains 73,101 episodes across 279 tasks, totaling 1,919.3 hours of bimanual robot teleoperation. Demonstrations are recorded at 30 Hz with left-wrist, right-wrist, and top-view RGB cameras. The egocentric human corpus contains 175,541 episodes across 327 tasks, totaling 993.9 hours, with single head-mounted RGB camera and tracked hand motion retargeted to 22-DoF dexterous-hand joint targets per hand. Together, the two sources comprise 248,642 episodes and 2,913.2 hours. The human camera view is replicated across the three input slots; each training 18 window is paired with its episode-level instruction and aligned program slice. Table 7 reports detailed statistics. Table 7: Pretraining Corpus Statistics. Episodes Durations (h) Tasks Total subtask slices Mean subtask slices per episode YAM 73,101 1,919.30 279 986,314 13.5 Egocentric Human 175,541 993.91 327 1,089,059 6.2 Total 248,642 2,913.22 606 2,075,373 8. B.2 SKILL LIBRARY DEFINITIONS skill is reusable motion that the model can invoke by name. Each skill is Python function written over the primitive API described in Appendix K.1, taking the objects it acts on as arguments, so that subtask recurring across the corpus becomes single call rather than being spelled out primitive by primitive. Following the annotation pipeline of Section 2.3, we generate skill library for each dataset: 23 skills for YAM and 27 skills for the egocentric human data. Tables 8 and 9 list them, each with one-line description of the motion it implements. Table 8: The Frozen YAM Skill Library (23 skills). Press the fabric flat with one arm and come off, then the other the alternating pats of smoothing slice. Brace the body with one arm, take its lid, flap or handle with the other, draw it open, then release the brace. Grip the same part twice, low to keep it aligned and high to push, and drive it home into its receptacle. Lift held flat object clear, roll the wrist half turn, release it inverted, then grasp it again to pin it down. Both arms pinch cloth edge, carry it across the item, and release one fold. Open the idle arm, then pick the object up with the working arm. Two grippullrelease bites that walk long object out of bag, sleeve or slot. Hover the carried object above detected target at the current wrist orientation and lower it in; the caller releases. Grip part where it sits, drag it straight off along one bounded delta, and release. Grip drawer, lid, door or cover and drive it along its travel until shut, then let go. Two ratchet strokes on threaded fastener; the release in between is the wrist unwinding, not drop. Two ratchet bites on threaded part; the sign of the angle sets whether it tightens or loosens. One-arm transport inside single slice: pick the object up and place it at the named target. One reach-limited bite of rolling: pinch, push the roll forward, release, and travel back to the next pinch point. Pin the case with one arm, take the zipper pull with the other, and draw it one run along the seam. Pin the parent sheet, roll or bag with one arm, pinch the piece with the other, and pull along the tear line. Carry held vessel over detected receptacle, clear the rim, tip once, and return to upright. Two hand-over-hand bites on strand being wound: regrasp further along and pull the slack taut, twice. Twist threaded part, let the wrist unwind and re-close, twist again, and lift the freed part clear. Park cloth or sponge already in one hand on an open surface and run two out-and-back strokes. Lead held wrapper ribbon, foil, film, gauze once around target in closed circuit. B.3 VISUALIZATIONS OF YAM SKILLS We visualize four of the 23 YAM skills. For each, we select one representative slice and show strip of key frames, the corresponding task and subgoal annotations, the program slice, and the skill function. In the listings, calls in bold are library skills; all others are primitive calls. Skill I: fold edge over Task: wrap blanket roll with ribbon Sub-goal: Fold the blanket at the center of the board Figure 8: Key frames of Skill I, fold edge over. Skill definition: def fold_edge_over(robot, item_name, left_delta, right_delta): # pinch the edge with both arms robot.grasp(item_name, left) robot.grasp(item_name, right) # carry the pinched edge across the item robot.servo_ee_delta(left, left_delta) robot.servo_ee_delta(right, right_delta) # let the fold lie robot.release(left) robot.release(right) Program slice for this episode: fold_edge_over(robot, blanket, [0.15, 0.0, 0.0], [0.15, 0.0, 0.0]) Skill II: alternating smoothing pats Task: roll towels Sub-goal: Flatten the towel Figure 9: Key frames of Skill II, alternating smoothing pats. Skill definition: def alternating_smoothing_pats(robot, fabric_name, first_side, second_side): # pat 1 -- press the fabric flat, then come off robot.grasp(fabric_name, first_side) robot.release(first_side) # pat 2 -- the other hand, on the other half of the sheet robot.grasp(fabric_name, second_side) robot.release(second_side) Program slice for this episode: # Smooth out the towel with alternating pats alternating_smoothing_pats(robot, towel, left, right) Skill III: flip object over Task: fold napkin into case and place utensils in it Sub-goal: Turn over the spoon at the center of the board Figure 10: Key frames of Skill III, flip object over. Skill definition: def flip_object_over(robot, object_name, side, lift_delta, turn_deg=180.0): # lift just clear so the object can swing robot.servo_ee_delta(side, lift_delta) # roll the wrist -- this is the flip robot.rotate(object_name, turn_deg, side) # let it fall the last centimetre, landing inverted robot.release(side) # pin the flipped object down again for the next slice robot.grasp(object_name, side) Program slice for this episode: # Lift, roll the wrist to flip the spoon, drop it, and pin it flip_object_over(robot, spoon, left, [0.0, 0.0, 0.1]) 22 Skill IV: adjust in place Task: place bookmark into book Sub-goal: Adjust the bookmark in the book Figure 11: Key frames of Skill IV, adjust in place. Skill definition: def adjust_in_place(robot, object_name, side, nudge_delta): # take hold where it sits -- no lift robot.grasp(object_name, side) # slide it by small bounded amount robot.servo_ee_delta(side, nudge_delta) # let it settle robot.release(side) Program slice for this episode: adjust_in_place(robot, bookmark, right, [0.05, 0.0, 0.0]) B.4 VISUALIZATIONS OF EGOCENTRIC HUMAN SKILLS We visualize six of the 27 egocentric human skills. For each, we select one representative slice and show strip of key frames, the corresponding task and sub-goal annotations, the program slice, and the skill function. In the listings, calls in bold are library skills; all others are primitive calls. Skill I: open closure Task: assemble photo album Sub-goal: Open the photo album Figure 12: Key frames of Skill I, open closure. Skill definition: def open_closure(robot, container_name, closure_name, side, brace_side, axis, angle_deg): # Hold the container body down so the closure, not the container, moves. robot.grasp(container_name, brace_side) # Take the closure where it sits. robot.grasp(closure_name, side) # Swing it open about its hinge. robot.rotate(closure_name, axis, angle_deg, side) # Come off the closure; it stays open. robot.release(side) Program slice for this episode: open_closure(robot, photo album, photo album cover, left, right, object_long, 180.0) 23 Skill II: pour into target Task: serve rice into bowl Sub-goal: Pour spoonful of rice into the bowl Figure 13: Key frames of Skill II, pour into target. Skill definition: def pour_into_target(robot, vessel_name, target_name, side, axis, angle_deg): # Bring the held vessels mouth over the receiving target. robot.goto_relative(side, target_name, above) # Tip it until it pours. robot.rotate(vessel_name, axis, angle_deg, side) # Bring it back upright; the pour ends. robot.rotate(vessel_name, axis, -angle_deg, side) Program slice for this episode: pour_into_target(robot, spoon, bowl, right, object_long, 110.0) Skill III: stir contents Task: mixing solutions with stirring rod Sub-goal: Stir the solution in the beaker Figure 14: Key frames of Skill III, stir contents. Skill definition: def stir_contents(robot, tool_name, vessel_name, side): # Bring the held tool down inside the vessel, among the contents. robot.goto_relative(side, vessel_name, inside) # Sweep it round the vessel; the grip never changes, nothing is let go. robot.rotate(tool_name, vertical, 360.0, side) robot.rotate(tool_name, vertical, 360.0, side) Program slice for this episode: brace_and_take_tool(robot, beaker, left, stirring rod, right) stir_contents(robot, stirring rod, beaker, right) Skill IV: wipe surface back and forth Task: use lint roller on pants Sub-goal: Remove the lint from the pair of pants Figure 15: Key frames of Skill IV, wipe surface back and forth. Skill definition: def wipe_surface_back_and_forth(robot, surface_name, relation, stroke_direction, return_direction, side): # Park the cloth on the surface. robot.goto_relative(side, surface_name, relation) # Out and back. robot.move_arm(side, stroke_direction) robot.move_arm(side, return_direction) # And again. robot.move_arm(side, stroke_direction) robot.move_arm(side, return_direction) Program slice for this episode: # Roll the lint roller back and forth over the pants (4 pairs of strokes) for _ in range(2): wipe_surface_back_and_forth(robot, pants, against, right, left, left) Skill V: fold over and crease Task: fold long pants Sub-goal: Fold pair of pants Figure 16: Key frames of Skill V, fold over and crease. Skill definition: def fold_over_and_crease(robot, item_name, side, brace_side, direction, fold_direction): # Hold the item down so the fold, not the whole item, travels. robot.grasp(item_name, brace_side) # Take the free edge with the working hand. robot.grasp(item_name, side) # Carry the edge across the item ... robot.move_arm(side, direction) # ... and land it on the far side. robot.move_arm(side, fold_direction) # Let the folded edge down. robot.release(side) # Press the crease flat. robot.press(item_name, side) Program slice for this episode: fold_over_and_crease(robot, pants, left, right, up, right) 25 Skill VI: wrap around target Task: use curling iron to curl hair Sub-goal: Wrap section of hair around the curling iron Figure 17: Key frames of Skill VI, wrap around target. Skill definition: def wrap_around_target(robot, target_name, side): # Start over the top of the target. robot.goto_relative(side, target_name, above) # Over the far side. robot.move_arm(side, away_from_body) # Down its far face. robot.move_arm(side, down) # Back underneath, toward the body. robot.move_arm(side, toward_body) # And up to close the circuit. robot.move_arm(side, up) Program slice for this episode: # Wrap the hair around the curling iron twice. for _ in range(2): wrap_around_target(robot, curling iron, left) B.5 SKILL DISTRIBUTION IN THE EMBEDDING SPACE In Figure 18 and 19, we visualize the skill distribution of variant skills in the pretrained code experts embedding space. Each point represents one episode slice, placed by two-dimensional t-SNE projection of its embedding and colored by the skill assigned to it. Dashed outlines mark the region covered by each skill, and the frames along the edges show representative short span from an episode for selected skills. Figure 18 covers the 18 most common skills in the YAM library and Figure 19 the 16 most common skills in the egocentric human library. In both, slices assigned to different skills occupy largely separate regions, suggesting that the skill label is predictive of the motion in slice and can serve as conditioning signal for action generation. 26 Figure 18: Skills of the YAM Skill Library in the Embedding Space. Figure 19: Skills of the Egocentric Human Skill Library in the Embedding Space.

sections.title: C BASELINE IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: In Sections 3.1 and 3.2, we compare AW-0 with four baselines: π0.5, DreamZero, EgoScale, and WLA. Here, we describe how each is reproduced and adapted. On RoboTwin 2.0, we train single multi-task policy per baseline on 2,500 demo clean demonstrations (50 tasks 50 demonstrations). For each of the 8 real-world tasks, we train separate policy per baseline using task-specific demonstrations sampled at 30 Hz. Every baseline receives language instruction, the robot state, and three RGB views (one head and two wrist cameras). All baselines follow the same evaluation protocol as AW-0. All real-world rollouts are scored using the task-specific rubrics in Appendix E. π0.5 (Black et al., 2025) is vision-language-action model that combines pretrained visionlanguage backbone with flow-matching action expert. We follow the official OpenPI implementation2 and initialize all policies from the released π0.5 pretrained checkpoint. For each real-world task, we fine-tune separate policy for 50 epochs on the task-specific demonstrations. We use 14-dimensional joint-space actions on RoboTwin and YAM, and 62-dimensional actions on Tianji Sharpa consisting of 9-dimensional end-effector pose and 22 hand joints per side. Arm actions are relative to the current state, while gripper and hand actions are absolute targets. We reinitialize the action input and output projections to accommodate these dimensions and fine-tune all model parameters. Following the official implementation, we use an action horizon of 50 for RoboTwin and 32 for the real robots, together with quantile normalization and standard image augmentation. All models are trained with AdamW on eight H100 GPUs using FSDP and global batch size of 256. We use peak learning rate of 5 105 with cosine decay to 5 106 and 2,000 warmup steps. DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) is world-action model that jointly generates future video and actions using pretrained video diffusion backbone. We follow the official implementation3 and initialize from the DreamZero-AgiBot checkpoint. We reproduce DreamZero on RoboTwin and all 8 realworld tasks, training separate policy for 10 epochs on each real-world task. We fully fine-tune the diffusion transformer and state/action modules, while keeping the text encoder, image encoder, and video VAE frozen. Following the original design, the three camera views are tiled into one frame, and each training sample contains up to four action chunks of 24 steps. Actions are predicted relative 2https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi 3https://github.com/dreamzero0/dreamzero 27 to the state at the beginning of each chunk, with absolute hand-joint targets on TianjiSharpa. The state and action projections are adapted to the target embodiment, and the video and action losses are weighted equally. All policies are trained with AdamW on 32 H100 GPUs using global batch size of 32. We use the same training hyperparameters across all tasks, with peak learning rate of 2 105 and 5% linear warmup followed by cosine decay. EgoScale (using the GR00T N1.7-3B checkpoint) (Zheng et al., 2026) studies how pretraining on egocentric human demonstrations scales to dexterous robot manipulation. We reproduce this baseline using the GR00T N1.7 implementation4 and initialize from the pretrained nvidia/GR00T-N1.7-3B checkpoint. For each real-world task, we fine-tune separate policy for 50 epochs while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen and training the projection layers and diffusion action head. We use relative joint actions for the arms on RoboTwin and YAM, relative end-effector actions on TianjiSharpa, and absolute targets for the grippers and 22-DoF dexterous hands. Following the official fine-tuning recipe, we apply state dropout with probability 0.2, random image cropping, and color jitter. We use an action horizon of 20 steps and train with AdamW on eight H100 GPUs with global batch size of 640. The peak learning rate is 104, with 5% linear warmup followed by cosine decay and weight decay of 105. WLA (Yang et al., 2026) combines vision-language backbone, world expert, and an action expert to jointly model visual observations, language, and robot actions. We follow the official implementation5 and initialize the backbone and world expert from pretrained RynnBrain-2B and Sana-600M weights, respectively. The connector and action expert are randomly initialized. We train separate policy for 50 epochs on each real-world task, updating all modules except the image VAE. Following the original design, the policy observes the current head and wrist views together with the head view from 8 steps earlier. We use 64 meta-queries and 32-step action chunk, with absolute action targets normalized to [1, 1]. The world expert predicts the head-camera image at the end of the chunk, and its flow-matching loss is weighted by 0.1 relative to the action loss. All models are trained with AdamW on eight H100 GPUs using global batch size of 256. We use peak learning rate of 5 105 with cosine decay to 5 106 and 1,000 warmup steps. REAL-WORLD EXPERIMENTAL SETUP We conduct data collection and policy evaluation on two robot embodiments: the YAM station with parallel grippers and the TianjiSharpa station with dexterous hands. This section describes the robot hardware, visual observations, and teleoperation interfaces used in our experiments. Figure 20 gives an overview of the two stations. Robot Hardware and Control. The YAM station is fixed-base bimanual system with two 6-DoF arms, each equipped with parallel gripper. The TianjiSharpa station consists of Tianji humanoid torso with two arms and two 22-DoF Sharpa dexterous hands. For AW-0, both embodiments use the 64-dimensional stateaction representation described in Appendix A. The policy predicts relative end-effector poses together with absolute gripper targets on YAM or absolute finger-joint targets on TianjiSharpa. Perception System. Both stations provide three RGB views: head or overhead camera observes the tabletop workspace, and camera at each wrist provides local view of the gripper or hand and the manipulated objects. Each policy receives these images together with the task instruction and robot state. For AW-0, images are resized to 224 320 pixels, and the state contains the end-effector poses and the gripper positions or hand-joint angles. The same camera streams are provided to all baselines, with method-specific preprocessing described in Appendix C. Teleoperation and Data Collection. We collect YAM demonstrations using the standard YAM station configuration, with two master arms and two puppet arms. The operator moves the master arms, whose measured joint angles are sent as joint-position targets to the corresponding puppet arms. The triggers on the teaching handles control the parallel gripper openings, yielding six arm-joint targets and one gripper target per side. For TianjiSharpa, we use Manus gloves with PICO motion trackers attached to the gloves, together with an Apple Vision Pro worn around the operators neck. The tracked wrist positions and orientations define poses in SE(3), which are mapped to end-effector 4https://github.com/NVIDIA/Isaac-GR00T 5https://github.com/SJTU-DENG-Lab/WLA 28 (a) YAM Station (b) TianjiSharpa Station Figure 20: Real-world Robot Setups. (a) The YAM station: two arms with linear grippers, with RealSense D405 camera overhead and one on each wrist. The bottom camera is not used. (b) The TianjiSharpa station: Tianji torso with two Sharpa Wave dexterous hands, observed by an SHW5G camera on the head and one on each wrist. targets for the two Tianji arms. In parallel, finger-motion measurements from the Manus gloves are retargeted to 22-dimensional joint-position targets for each Sharpa hand. At each teleoperation step, the arm-pose and hand-joint targets are passed to the corresponding robot controllers to coordinate arm and finger motion. During collection, we record the three RGB camera streams, measured robot states, and commanded action targets. We use their timestamps to pair visual observations with robot states and action commands, and associate each demonstration with task instruction for post-training. REAL-WORLD TASK PROGRESS We evaluate 8 real-world tasks that span two robot platforms. Arrange Fruits, Pack Backpack, Replace Lightbulb, and Fold and Stack Towels run on the YAM bimanual setup (two 6-DoF arms with parallel grippers); Arrange Fruits with Tongs, Deal Poker, Flip Scoreboard, and Solve Rubiks Cube run on the Tianji humanoid torso with two Sharpa dexterous hands. For each task we show the progress with the key frames of one training episode together with its code label; every color-coded block of the program is linked to the range of frames it explains. Each task is graded with an additive rubric that awards independent partial credit for each completed sub-step. E.1 YAM TASKS 29 Task I: Arrange Fruits. Figure 21: Key frames and code label of Arrange Fruits. Grading rubric (additive): +0.3: (a) Moves each fruit not named in the instruction from the left bowl into the right basket (or none to remove). +0.3: (b) Moves each named fruit not yet in the left bowl from the right basket into the bowl (or none to fetch). +0.4: (c) Final state matches the instruction and no fruit is dropped. 30 Task II: Pack Backpack. Figure 22: Key frames and code label of Pack Backpack. Grading rubric (additive): +0.15: (a) Left gripper grasps the zipper pull at the left end and slides it to the middle. +0.15: (b) Right gripper re-grasps the pull at the middle and slides it to the right end. +0.2: (c) Open the backpack with the left gripper. +0.2: (d) Picks up the item from the table and places it inside the open backpack. +0.15: (e) Right gripper grasps the pull at the right end and slides it back to the middle. +0.15: (f) Left gripper slides the pull from the middle to the left end; the backpack is fully closed with the item inside. 31 Task III: Replace Lightbulb. Figure 23: Key frames and code label of Replace Lightbulb. Condition dead bulb, replacement required. Grading rubric (additive): +0.1: (a) Left gripper presses the inline switch and the bulb stays dark. +0.1: (b) Left gripper braces the lamp base. +0.2: (c) Right gripper unscrews the dead bulb and lifts it out of the socket. +0.1: (d) Dead bulb is set down in the bulb tray. +0.1: (e) Right gripper picks up the spare bulb. +0.3: (f) Spare bulb is seated in the socket and screwed in clockwise until lit. +0.1: (g) When the bulb is lit, release both arms to their home positions. Condition working bulb, no replacement needed. Grading rubric (additive): +0.3: Left gripper presses the inline switch and the bulb lights up. +0.7: The lit bulb shows the lamp still works, so both arms move back to their initial pose and stay still until the episode ends. 32 Task IV: Fold and Stack Towels. Figure 24: Key frames and code label of Fold and Stack Towels. Grading rubric (additive): +0.2: (a) Grasps towel edge and completes one fold. +0.2: (b) Each of the three towels is folded flat. +0.1: (c) Picks folded towel up and lays it on the pile. +0.2: (d) All three folded towels end up in single pile, none dropped or left behind. +0.3: (e) The pile reads, bottom to top, in the colour order the instruction names. E.2 TIANJISHARPA TASKS 33 Task I: Arrange Fruits with Tongs. Figure 25: Key frames and code label of Arrange Fruits with Tongs. Grading rubric (additive): +0.2: (a) Right hand takes the tongs off their stand and keeps hold of them. +0.25: (b) Moves each fruit not named in the instruction from the left bowl into the tray (or none to remove). +0.25: (c) Moves each named fruit not yet in the left bowl from the tray into the bowl (or none to fetch). +0.2: (d) Final state matches the instruction and no fruit is dropped. +0.1: (e) Tongs are put back on their stand. 34 Task II: Deal Poker. sections.title: F ANALYSIS ON CODE GENERATION QUALITY
sections.content: F.1 PRE-TRAINED CODE GENERATION QUALITY We evaluate the pretrained code expert on the validation split of the pretraining dataset, before downstream task-specific fine-tuning. Table 10 reports quantitative metrics on this split, while Figures 29 36 and 30 present generated programs for YAM and egocentric human validation examples. We examine visual grounding, program structure, and semantic agreement with the reference annotations. Table 10: Validation Metrics for the Pretrained Code Expert. TF denotes teacher-forced evaluation. The grounding gap is the absolute increase in code loss when visual observations are shuffled across validation samples. TF loss 0.535 TF accuracy 0.897 Grounding gap 1.774 Parse rate 0.875 Entity F1 0.534 Primitive F1 0.365 Skill-call rate 0.292 Quantitative Assessment. The model achieves 89.7% teacher-forced token accuracy and an 87.5% parse rate under free generation. Shuffling visual observations increases the code loss by 1.774, indicating that code prediction depends on the visual context. Entity and primitive F1 are 0.534 and 0.365, respectively, measuring overlap of quoted strings and robot API names with the reference programs. These scores indicate partial semantic agreement despite the higher syntactic validity. In addition, 29.2% of generated programs contain skill-style helper calls, identified by calls that take robot as their first argument. Together, these results show that pretraining learns visually conditioned program generation and skill invocation, while precise semantic and argument prediction remain areas for improvement. YAM Robot Demonstrations. Figure 29 shows held-out YAM demonstration of Clean keyboard with cloth. The generated program expresses cloth handover followed by repeated scrubbing through scrub back and forth, preserving the object arguments, arm assignment, and loop structure of the reference subtask. This illustrates how reusable skill can encode repeated motion compactly. The generated displacement argument nevertheless contains two extra entries, illustrating that an appropriate skill-level plan can still contain parameter errors that prevent reliable direct execution. Figure 29: Pretrained Code Generation on YAM Validation Example. The generated program is compared with reference program from another labeled episode of the same task. Egocentric Human Demonstrations. Figure 30 illustrates subtask-level planning under the instruction Squeeze toothpaste. The generated program describes the preparatory subtask of removing the cap: stabilizing the tube, repeatedly twisting the cap, and lifting it away. It matches the annotated calls, arguments, and loop structure for this validation window. ADDITIONAL ANALYSIS ON REAL-WORLD RESULTS G. IMPACT OF CODE EXPERT ON LANGUAGE FOLLOWING CAPABILITY We further examine whether code-based planning improves the alignment of predicted visual dynamics with task semantics. As shown in Figure 33, we compare the video generation quality of the right wrist camera of AW-0 with natural-language subgoal variant (Subgoal) and model without planning stream (AW-0 w/o code), under the instruction Arrange the fruits so that finally there is only mango in the left bowl. This task requires identifying the intended object and grounding the desired outcome in an appropriate interaction. The three variants are evaluated under the same task and scene configuration, with similar but non-identical initial observations from separate rollouts. The predicted futures reveal distinct differences in task understanding: AW-0 directs the interaction toward the mango, whereas Subgoal exhibits ambiguous targeting between the apple and mango, and AW-0 w/o code targets the apple. These observations suggest that structured skill calls and explicit object arguments provide more specific planning condition for video prediction than natural-language subgoal alone. By connecting instruction semantics to concrete interactions, the code stream helps align predicted dynamics with the intended task. Since the action expert also conditions on predictive video representations, this alignment provides pathway for improving language following, complementing the execution results in our main experiments. G.2 IMPACT OF CODE EXPERT ON SKILL ROBUSTNESS We further examine whether code-based planning improves the prediction of physical dynamics and skill robustness during precise manipulation. As shown in Figure 34, we compare the future frames predicted by AW-0, Subgoal, and AW-0 w/o code for the right wrist camera on Deal Poker, focusing on the final stage in which the right hand inserts card into slot. This interaction requires aligning the held card with the narrow opening and guiding it into the slot, making the relative motion of the hand, card, and receptacle critical to an accurate prediction. The three variants receive similar but non-identical initial observations sampled at nearby time steps from the same episode. The predicted futures reveal distinct differences in the insertion motion: AW-0 depicts the card aligning with and entering the slot more accurately, whereas Subgoal and AW-0 w/o code produce less coherent insertion sequences, with blur and distortions around the hand and manipulated objects. These observations suggest that explicit skill calls and object arguments help the video expert better predict how the hand and card should move relative to the receptacle. The implementation of the code expert supports more accurate video generation, and therefore provides the action expert with more reliable predictive guidance for precise manipulation. sections.title: I HYBRID ACTIONS ALGORITHM
sections.content: Algorithms 1 and 2 outline the workflow of the hybrid mode. From an observation and instruction ℓ, one forward pass of the policy π returns direct action chunk a1:H over the replan horizon and code slice c. Every slice executes in shared namespace containing the environments skill API, reusable helper definitions, and its setup block (episode-start perception), which persists throughout the episode. At each replanning point, ARBITRATE decides which of the two channels drives the robot. The returned flag indicates whether code execution was attempted, not whether it succeeded. If execution is attempted, the action chunk from the same policy invocation is discarded, even if an exception occurs; the next iteration observes the current state and replans. Otherwise, the chunk is played for steps as in the default mode. The original generated slice is checked without repair. It is executed only if it passes the following gates in order: 1. Stage Gate: its stage is not complete, is not below stage already attempted, and has fewer than failed execution attempts; 2. Dependency Gate: every variable it reads is defined in G; and 3. Syntax, Whitelist, and Vacuity Gates: it compiles as generated, calls only whitelisted functions, and contains an executable statement.

During hybrid evaluation, generated code executes through perception and control primitives implemented using Molmo for visual grounding (Deitke et al., 2024), SAM 3 for segmentation (Carion et al., 2025), Contact-GraspNet for grasp generation (Sundermeyer et al., 2021), and RoboTwins native motion-planning and gripper-control interfaces (Chen et al., 2025). Neither the generated programs nor the underlying primitives access privileged simulator information during evaluation. For demonstration collection, we preserve the same API interface but use privileged object states and annotated grasps to improve collection efficiency. Scope of Comparison. The default and hybrid configurations differ in both their training demonstration collection pipelines and execution modes to support their training requirements. Unlike the default configuration, which uses demonstrations collected with RoboTwins native motion planner, the hybrid configuration uses CaP-based data collection because it naturally pairs each demonstration with an aligned program executable in the RoboTwin simulator, supporting the code execution component of hybrid actions. Therefore, our resulting comparison evaluates the two configuration as whole and does not isolate the effect of hybrid execution alone. Code and Action Usage. Table 12 reports the fraction of simulation steps driven by each of the two control channels during the hybrid evaluation in Table 1: execution of code produced by the code expert and direct action chunks generated by the action expert. On successful episodes, code drives 14.5% of steps in the clean setting and 35.0% in the random setting. The gap follows from Table 1. In the clean setting, the action expert alone is already strong (80.8%), so there is little for code to add. Admitting code in fact lowers success to 63.1%, which we attribute to the code channel inheriting the failure modes of the low-level perception and control primitives it calls, and the arbiter admits code slice on validity alone, without predicting whether it will outperform the action chunk it displaces. In the random setting, where direct action degrades to 20.6%, the code channel carries third of the physical time on the episodes that succeed and lifts success to 29.2%. Executing the code experts generation thus complements the action expert especially where learned actions are less reliable, here under visually out-of-distribution scenes. Pooled over all episodes, code execution accounts for only 8.5% of steps in the clean setting and 5.6% in the random setting. The pooled share is dominated by failed episodes, which run to the step cap and accumulate roughly five times as many steps as successful ones (52.7k vs. 11.5k in clean, 55.5k vs. 8.4k in random), almost all under direct action. Qualitative Examples of CodeAction Interleaving. Figure 37 shows two qualitative examples of how code execution and direct action generation interleave within an episode. The top progress bar shows an episode of blocks ranking rgb, where the three blocks must be arranged in row in red, green, blue order. We observe that the three pick-and-place cycles are almost entirely carried out by code execution, with direct action generation taking over around stage transition. For tasks of this kind that involve regularly shaped objects and well-structured motions, the integration is able to utilize the stable and smooth behavior yields by the CaP actions. The bottom progress bar shows an episode of pick dual bottles, where the two bottles must be picked up and held together. Here, code execution correctly localized the bottle and moves the gripper to it but fails to secure the grasp due to its less regular shape. Direct action generated from the model then takes over and completes the grasp, after which code execution resumes to finish the episode.

sections.title: L LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Program Grounding and Skill Coverage. The code stream learns from automatically annotated demonstrations and curated skill library, making its planning quality dependent on annotation accuracy and skill coverage. Generated programs can select an appropriate skill yet contain incorrect arguments, as illustrated in Appendix F.1; syntactic validity therefore does not ensure correct execution. Future work could use execution feedback to improve program grounding and discover or refine reusable skills beyond the initial library. Predictive Robustness and Hybrid Execution. Structured planning improves WAM performance but does not eliminate sensitivity to visual distribution shifts. Hybrid execution improves robustness under RoboTwin randomization, yet reduces clean-setting performance (Appendix J.2). This tradeoff reflects both the reliability of the underlying primitives and the limitation of selecting code based on validity without estimating its advantage over the action chunk. Learning to arbitrate using execution reliability and expected task progress could better exploit the complementary strengths of the two modes. Toward Continual Agentic Learning. Our real-world hybrid evaluation is limited to YAM platform due to the lack of code-as-policy systems for dexterous hand, and the current system does not learn online from its own interactions. The unified design nevertheless offers basis for coupling program generation and world prediction with execution feedback and model updates. Future work could explore iterative plan revision, skill-library expansion, and autonomous learning through sustained environmental interaction, with broader evaluation across tasks and embodiments.
